parts.title: How brain cells mix up their predictions and their mistakes
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Groups of nerve cells in the brain build an inner 'world model': a mental picture of how things work, which helps guide what we do. One idea, called predictive processing, says that a telltale sign of this inner model is that nerve cells do two jobs at once. Some carry signals that predict what the senses will tell us, and at the same time the network works out the prediction errors, which are the gaps between what we expected and what actually happens.

We wanted to understand how the brain makes predictions when it has to handle many signals at once, some from the senses and some from our own movements. To do this, we studied computer models of brain networks in which nerve cells are connected to each other in loops, so that each cell's activity feeds back on the others. We asked how these networks come to hold predictions that involve many signals at once, from more than one sense.

Earlier ideas suggested that the brain uses separate kinds of cells for separate jobs. We found the opposite. In networks that make reliable predictions, the signals that stand for the outside world and the signals that stand for prediction errors are mixed together, not kept apart. We confirmed this prediction of our model by giving animals a rich set of signals and then breaking their learned expectations.

We also propose that predictions work best when the balance between excitatory and inhibitory signals is loose. Excitatory signals push a cell to fire, and inhibitory signals hold it back. We show that excitatory and inhibitory nerve cells play different roles. Taken together, our results show that the brain's inner model is spread across many cells, yet arranged in a way that makes it easy to pull out the information that matters for behavior. Our results help explain how the brain builds its inner models, by bringing several different calculations together in one shared model.

Subject terms: Network models, Neural encoding, Sensorimotor processing, Cortex, Complex networks
parts.introduction_first:
Predictive processing means working out what the senses, our own movements, and other parts of a task are likely to be. It is thought to be one of the most basic things the brain does. When what we actually experience differs from what we expected, we get a prediction error. This mismatch is an important signal for the brain, because it can guide learning and the way connections between nerve cells change over time. Signs of predictive processing, including the brain activity that goes along with prediction errors, have been found in many brain circuits and in many kinds of animals.

Two well-studied kinds of experiments on predictive processing in the mouse cortex are ones that pair movement with sound, and ones that pair sight with sound. The cortex is the outer layer of the brain, and the cortex is where these experiments take place. Earlier work proposed that a standard, small-scale circuit in the cortex is what the brain uses to make predictions and prediction errors. Some predictions about this circuit have been confirmed in particular situations. However, the idea that this same circuit pattern is the general way the brain makes predictions faces several challenges.
parts.introduction_rest:
There are three main gaps in what we know. First, most experiments on predictive processing train animals to learn just one link, such as one sound paired with one movement. In real life, though, the links between what we sense and what we do usually involve many signals at once. Speaking is one example. These links also depend on the situation. We know little about how particular arrangements of nerve cells in the brain learn to handle such many-signal calculations that combine more than one sense.

Second, predictive processing of signals from more than one sense has also been seen in several brain circuits outside the mammalian cortex. One example is a circuit deep in the brain that lies below the cortex. It is involved in placebo analgesia, where a person's belief that they are getting a painkiller can reduce their pain, so the circuit uses a prediction to turn pain down. Another example comes from cephalopods, such as octopuses. Their circuits that connect movement with sight predict how the animal looks to someone watching it from outside, and they use this prediction to produce camouflage patterns that involve many signals at once. We do not know whether these circuits make predictions from several senses in the same way as the mammalian cortex, or in completely different ways.

Third, the time it takes for a brain network to build up a prediction varies a lot. It can take about 1 minute, about 1 hour, or even days. This suggests that predictive processing is supported by plasticity, meaning the brain's ability to change its connections, and that this plasticity works over a range of time spans. Short-term plasticity, which changes connections over seconds to minutes, may be one of them. It also suggests that a circuit may not always need to be reorganized to make predictions.

There is good evidence that what the senses tell us is strongly shaped by what we predict. This has inspired many studies that use theory. Early work proposed that predictive coding, a way of making predictions in which the brain sends its predictions forward and its mistakes backward, may explain how nerve cells in the visual system respond. Each of these cells responds to a small patch of the scene, called its receptive field, and the early models tried to explain the properties of these patches when animals see natural pictures. These models are called autoencoders. They take a signal, squeeze it down to a compact summary, and then rebuild it. They are nonlinear, which means they can capture effects that are not simple sums. They can be read as the brain working out the hidden causes behind what the senses pick up. This fits with a Bayesian view, in which the brain combines what it already expects with what it actually senses.

Later work extended these models to explain brain activity that goes along with prediction errors. It showed that the balance between excitatory and inhibitory signals plays a part in producing these signals. However, these studies usually look at either predictions that combine only a few pairs of signals, or predictions that involve many signals but come from just one sense. Most comparisons have also been made against rough, large-scale measurements of brain activity, such as recordings of electrical signals from many cells at once or brain scans.

New experiments are starting to show how our own movements, and how signals from different senses affect each other, shape what the brain represents. Even so, we still do not understand, at the level of single cells and whole circuits, how the brain makes these predictions that combine many signals from several senses. This makes it hard to test ideas about how the circuits do these calculations against modern recordings that measure large numbers of nerve cells.

Another big gap, for both experiments and models, is predictive processing that combines many signals from more than one sense. We have two questions. (i) In natural conditions, how does the brain represent signals and movements that can be predicted, and ones that cannot? In nature, signals come in rich sets that depend on each other in complicated ways, and these sets may involve several senses and several kinds of movement. (ii) How do circuits produce these representations? And how are they shaped by experience and by how complex the signals in the environment are, for example how many signals they involve? In particular, we do not know whether the circuits that make predictions from rich sets of signals from several senses are kept apart from each other in what they do. If they are, we also do not know whether this separation comes from learning, or whether it depends on different types of cells that can be told apart by the molecules they carry.

We tackle these questions by studying how networks of nerve cells connected in loops build up predictions when they handle many signals from more than one sense, both while they are learning and after they have learned. We also compare our model with recordings of single nerve cells and of groups of cells. Inspired by recent experiments, we focus on learning tasks that pair signals from different senses. In these tasks, the network learns to link several pairs of signals that are not related to each other, drawn from different senses and kinds of movement. We adapted the classic predictive coding framework to these paired signals from different senses, and we studied how nerve cells respond in a simplified model of a network.

To understand how the brain does this, we make new predictions about how tightly the balance between excitatory and inhibitory signals should be held when many signals are involved. We also shed light on how this balance helps cancel out interference between several signals that the network has learned. The balance is kept by processes that work over very different time spans. So our work will let us bring together things that seem unrelated into one shared model, such as predictions that change because of short-term or long-term plasticity.

To understand what the brain does, our model suggests that predictions from many signals in several senses are reliable when the signals that stand for the outside world and the signals that stand for prediction errors are mixed together at the level of single cells. Finally, we extend these results to look at the different roles that excitatory and inhibitory nerve cells play in making inner predictions. We also look at how predictions from several senses change over time, and how they differ between the layers of the network. These results help explain how different arrangements of nerve cells and different biological processes support predictions from many signals in several senses in the parts of the brain that handle the senses. They also give further experimental support to our model.

The analysis and results we present here take earlier studies of predictive processing and extend them to many signals from several senses, some from the senses and some from our own movements. They also produce new predictions that we confirmed using experimental data. We therefore believe that our work reveals principles of predictive processing that hold across different species and different parts of the brain in natural settings. It also offers a way to plan and analyze future experiments, using numbers, to uncover the brain circuits behind these calculations.
parts.methods:
## Methods

### Our model of a network with loops

Our network is made of N nerve cells. We describe how active each cell is by its firing rate, which is how many times per second it fires. Together, the firing rates of all the cells at time t form a list of numbers, called a vector: r(t) = (r1(t), …, rN(t)). The network is driven by a large number of signals from the outside world, which we call stimuli. We write them as x(t) = (x1(t), …, xP(t)) and y(t) = (y1(t), …, yP(t)). The vectors x and y stand for stimuli from two senses, and during training the two are paired.

The network's activity changes over time according to this equation:

(1) dh_i(t)/dt = −h_i(t) + b ∑_{j=1}^{N} J_ij ϕ(h_j(t)) + I_i^F(x(t), y(t))

Here h_i(t) is the voltage of each cell, and its firing rate is linked to that voltage by a nonlinear activation function, r_i(t) = ϕ(h_i(t)). An activation function is a rule that turns a cell's voltage into its firing rate. "Nonlinear" means the rule is not a simple straight line. In Eq. (1), the input each cell receives has two parts. The recurrent part, I_i^R, comes from other cells in the network. The feedforward part, I_i^F(x(t), y(t)), comes from the outside stimuli. We multiplied both the connection strengths J_ij and the feedforward input by a constant b. You can think of b as a gain: it sets how strongly the network responds.

We worked out the exact forms of J_ij and I_i^F(x(t), y(t)) using a normative approach. This means we started from the job the network is supposed to do and worked backwards to find the rules that do it best. The details of this derivation are in the Supplementary Information (SI) §2. We assume that the cells' activity together makes the following quantity as small as possible:

(2) E(t) = ∑_{k=1}^{P} [x_k(t+d) − x̂_k(t)]² + [y_k(t+d) − ŷ_k(t)]² + 2b ∑_{i=1}^{N} F(r_i(t))

The first part of E(t) is the prediction errors. It adds up the squared gaps between the stimuli that will arrive at time t+d and the network's own predictions, x̂(t) and ŷ(t), made at time t. The second part is the encoding efficiency. It adds up F(r) over all the cells. F(r) is a function that always goes up as r goes up, and its exact form depends on ϕ, the activation function (SI §2.1). For the ReLU activation function, ϕ(z) = max(z − θ, 0), F(r) = (r + θ)²/2. ReLU is a common rule in which a cell's output is zero when its input is below a threshold θ, and otherwise it is the input minus θ.

This is similar to earlier work on predictive coding for natural images [34, 35]. In that work, the nonlinear response of the cells acts as a regularization term, a penalty that keeps the network from becoming too complicated, and it controls the encoding efficiency. Here, we focus on networks that handle inputs from more than one sense. Making E(t) as small as possible is the same as doing Bayesian inference, a way of reasoning that weighs up what is likely given the evidence, to work out the hidden "cause" behind the sensory signals (SI §2.2). Our model is closely related to the classic Hopfield model for associative learning, which learns links between things. The difference is that it uses an anti-Hebbian learning rule [86], in which connections are strengthened when the two cells are not active together, the opposite of the usual rule. The value b in Eq. (2) controls a trade-off: the network has to balance making small prediction errors against keeping its encoding efficiency high.

We also assume that the network's predictions are simple averages of its activity:

(3) x̂_k(t) = (1/N) w_k · r(t),  ŷ_k(t) = (1/N) v_k · r(t)

Here w_k and v_k are readout weight vectors. Each is a list of N numbers that says how much each cell counts towards the prediction. By definition, these predictions are of future input, as the delay d in Eq. (2) shows. However, we focus on the case where the input changes much more slowly than the cells' firing rates. So, over the short time in which firing rates change [Eq. (1)], we treat the stimuli as roughly constant:

(4) x_k(t+d) ≈ x_k(t) ≈ x_k,  y_k(t+d) ≈ y_k(t) ≈ y_k

Eq. (4) does not mean the stimulus has to stay still. A stimulus that changes more slowly than the nerve cells' activity still fits this assumption. In that case, the cells' activity closely follows the changes in the stimulus. One special case is a stimulus that never changes. In the predictive processing literature, this kind of prediction is often called "spatial prediction" [57]. Our results apply to both cases: slowly changing stimuli and unchanging ones.

We assume that the weight vectors w_k and v_k change during learning so as to make E(t) [Eq. (2)] as small as possible. You can think of these changes as a mix of two things. The first is gradient descent on the squared prediction error in Eq. (2), which means nudging the weights step by step in whichever direction lowers the error fastest. The second is homeostatic plasticity (SI §2.1), a built-in tendency of the network to keep its weights at a steady overall size. These weight changes can come from local plasticity rules, which change each part of a cell's input separately, applied to the dendrites, the branches that receive signals (SI §2.3). This extends earlier findings in refs. 46 and 47.

If the weights start out at random, learning makes the weight vectors more correlated, meaning they become more alike (SI §2.1). In particular, we show that when the network is very large (N → ∞), the weights have these statistics:

(5) ⟨w_ik⟩ = ⟨v_ik⟩ = 0,  ⟨(w_ik)²⟩ = ⟨(v_ik)²⟩ = 1,  ⟨w_ik v_ik⟩ = μ_k

Here w_ik and v_ik are the individual entries of w_k and v_k. The angle brackets mean an average over the weights. Homeostatic plasticity keeps each weight's average at zero and its typical size (its variance) at one. The correlation between the two weights is μ_k, and it grows during learning, that is, as E gets smaller. To keep things simple, unless we say otherwise, all stimulus pairs have the same "age", so μ_k = μ does not depend on which pair k we look at. We also assume that the weights follow a multivariate Gaussian distribution, a bell-shaped spread that stretches over many numbers at once.

With these assumptions, we worked out exact formulas for how the steady-state firing rates depend on the stimuli and on the correlation μ. A steady state is the settled pattern the network reaches after it has learned. We did this in two limits (SI §3). In the high-dimensional case, both N and P are large, and their ratio α = P/N is a fixed number. In the low-dimensional case, only N is large, and α = 0. The problem we ended up with is generally nonconvex, which means it can have many different solutions, so the exact solution a single network reaches may depend on the random starting weights. Remarkably, however, the steady-state firing-rate pattern we derived does not depend on the starting weights. This makes it a reliable and direct way to compare what the model predicts with what experiments show.

To show whether each stimulus was present or absent, we set the matching entries of x and y to 0 or 1. For example, for the k-th stimulus pair, the mismatch and match conditions are:

(x_k, y_k) = (1, 0)  (x-only mismatch condition)
(x_k, y_k) = (0, 1)  (y-only mismatch condition)
(x_k, y_k) = (1, 1)  (match condition)

Our derivation of how the network responds (SI §2.1) also covers more complicated pairings, where one entry of x is not matched one-to-one with one entry of y. It also covers cases where the two senses have different numbers of signals. We extend these results further to cases where more than two stimuli are linked together (SI §2.3).

### How our network model relates to recurrent autoencoders

Our network model and its goal function [Eqs. (1) and (2)] may look like the regularized autoencoder models used in machine learning, especially recurrent autoencoders [87]. An autoencoder is a computer program that learns to compress information and then rebuild it. We want to stress that our model differs from these models in several key ways:

In our work, the nerve cells' activity itself can be seen as doing Bayesian inference on hidden variables (SI §2.2). In recurrent autoencoders, by contrast, the hidden variables are stored in a separate set of "auxiliary" variables that are not the nerve cells' activity themselves [87]. Adding a separate set of variables might make this kind of model harder to interpret in terms of how the brain works.

In recurrent autoencoders, the network has to make an accurate prediction of the stimulus at every moment in time [87]. Our model has a looser rule: it only has to make predictions once it has reached a steady state.

Our network can learn to make predictions using local plasticity rules (SI §2.3.2). We expect the network structure that grows out of these local rules to produce nerve-cell patterns and circuit layouts that are different from those learned by back-propagation-through-time, the method commonly used to train recurrent autoencoders. Back-propagation-through-time works out how much each cell's activity contributed to the error, even though that contribution happened many time steps earlier.

In this work, we focus on the nerve-cell patterns and circuit mechanisms that support predictions involving many signals at once, from more than one sense, in the brain. We also link our network model to experimental data that probe the matching nerve-cell circuits.

### How stimuli, predictions and prediction errors are arranged

Under the assumptions above, the steady-state pattern of nerve-cell activity [Eq. (1)] can be written as:

(6) r ∝ a_x(μ) x + a_y(μ) y + α · noise

The symbol ∝ means "is proportional to". This form is revealing. The vectors a_x(μ) and a_y(μ) depend on the stimulus and on μ. They point in the directions along which the network encodes the stimuli in the x-only and y-only mismatch conditions. Eq. (6) also shows that, because of the nonlinearity, the network's response in the match condition is not simply a_x(μ) + a_y(μ). Fig. 1d shows how stimuli are arranged in the match and mismatch conditions. As training goes on and μ increases, these vectors change, and these changes show how the network's patterns for stimuli and prediction errors are learned. We also note that the size of the noise in Eq. (6) depends on the number of signals α, so it captures how the learned stimuli interfere with each other.

### What we mean by the balance level

At a steady state, the balance level of cell i is defined as:

(7) B_i = I_i^F / I_i^R

Here I_i^F and I_i^R are the feedforward and recurrent input currents to cell i at a steady state [Eq. (1)]. The balance level differs between cells and between stimuli, because the weights w_ik and v_ik are different for different cells (labelled by i) and different stimuli (labelled by k). We worked out the spread of balance levels, and its median, shown in Fig. 2, using exact formulas (SI §3.3). The median is the middle value when all the values are lined up in order.

In cases where the stimuli and the nerve-cell responses change over time (Figs. S6 and S7), we define the balance level of cell i at each moment in the same way:

(8) B_i(t) = I_i^F(t) / h_i(t)

Here I_i^F(t) is the outside input to cell i at time t, and h_i(t) is the voltage of cell i at time t. At a steady state, this gives the same result as Eq. (7).

### Finding the best balance level from experimental data

#### The movement–vision (V-M) experiment, ref. 20

We took the average voltage of all the recorded L2/3 nerve cells over many trials, plotted against time (Fig. 3a). L2/3 is a layer of the cortex. We measured each cell's voltage relative to its own baseline. We then collected 50 voltage values from all the recorded cells and all time points in the match and mismatch time windows (Fig. 3a). The match window ran from −0.1 to 0 s, and the mismatch window from 0 to 0.1 s. The time t = 0 is the moment when, in virtual reality, the treadmill was disconnected from the moving visual scene.

Next, we worked out the standard deviation of those 50 voltage values in the match and mismatch conditions. The standard deviation measures how spread out a set of values is. Dividing one standard deviation by the other gives a number without units that has a direct match in our model: the standard deviation of h_i over the cells in the network in Eq. (1). For P = 1 and θ = 0, we worked out this ratio exactly (SI §3):

(9) σ_mismatch² / σ_match² = [1/(2μ²) + (1 − μ²)/(1 + b/2)²] / [μ² + μ + (1 − μ²)[1 + b + (1 − μ)b²/4]]

We used μ = 0.97 as the correlation after training. We then adjusted the value of b until the formula matched the ratio measured in the data. Using the best-matching value, b*, we worked out the median balance level B* in the network model (Fig. 3c).

#### The active–movement (A-M) experiment, ref. 12

We took the average firing rates over many trials for all 815 regular spiking nerve cells, which are a common type of excitatory cell. We did this in the passive (mismatch) and movement (match) conditions, over two time windows: from t = −0.1 s to the start of the stimulus (t = 0), and from the start of the stimulus to t = 0.06 s (Fig. 3b). For each cell, we worked out how its firing rate changed between the two windows in each condition. We then drew 400 of these firing-rate changes from the 815 cells, allowing the same cell to be picked more than once, and calculated the average change in the passive and movement conditions.

We calculated the matching quantity in the model, which is the average of ϕ(h_i) over the cells in the network [Eq. (1)] in the match and mismatch conditions. For the ReLU activation function, the ratio is again given by Eq. (9), and we adjusted b until it matched the ratio measured in the data. Once more, we worked out the median balance level B* from the best-matching value b*. We repeated this fitting 100 times for both experiments, which gave the scatter plot of the estimated B* values in Fig. 3c.

### How we sorted cells into types

We call the steady-state voltage of cell i in the mismatch conditions h_ix (x-only) and h_iy (y-only), and in the match condition h_ixy. To sort cells into types, we compared how far each cell's voltage sat from the average with the standard deviation (σ) of the steady-state voltages. We measured σ using the voltages in the x-only mismatch condition after learning (μ = 0.97).

A cell i is a representation (R) neuron for the x-stimulus if it becomes more excited when the stimulus x is shown. In other words, its voltage in the x-only mismatch condition is high, and its voltages in the match and mismatch conditions are similar. In mathematical form:

(10) h_ix > σ/2  and  h_ix − h_ixy < σ/2

We used a similar rule to find R neurons for the y-stimulus. A cell i is a prediction-error (PE) neuron if it signals the "mismatch" between x and y. That is, its voltage in the x-only mismatch condition is high, and its voltage in the match condition is low. In mathematical form:

(11) h_ix > σ/2  and  h_ix − h_ixy > σ/2

We call cells that meet these rules positive PE neurons, because their activity goes up when x is shown but not expected (based on y). Negative PE neurons do the opposite: their activity goes up when x is not shown but is expected. In the model, when α = 0, the voltages of E neurons are spread around zero, so we applied the threshold to the voltage itself. When the network's activity changes over time (Figs. 5 and S6), we worked out the cell types [Eqs. (10) and (11)] at every moment, using the voltage h_i(t) in each stimulus condition, with the same fixed threshold σ.

For excitatory neurons in the high-dimensional case (α > 0) and for inhibitory neurons, the voltages are spread around a value other than zero. So for these cells, we used the voltages after subtracting their average (h_ix, h_ixy) in the rules above.

Some cells in the network may not fit any of these three types (Fig. S3a). We worked out the firing-rate statistics of the network's cells using exact formulas (SI §3 and 4). This let us find the share of R and PE neurons for different values of μ and α, shown in Fig. 4b, d. We also looked at how the choice of threshold affects the share of each cell type in Fig. S3b.

### Measuring how well the brain keeps signals apart, using responses to many stimuli in experiments

We took the average change in each cell's firing rate over many trials in the match (active) and mismatch (passive) conditions, separately for each sound stimulus in our experimental data [13]. To calculate a segregation index for each type of test sound, we looked only at cells that responded in the passive condition to that test sound and to the learned (expected) sound. We counted a cell as responsive if its firing rate was one half of the standard deviation above the average firing rate for the expected sound in the passive condition. Changing this threshold does not change the results in Fig. 4e, f.

For these cells, we worked out pairs of Δ values, each the difference between the mismatch and match responses, one for the test sound and one for the expected sound. The Pearson correlation coefficient between these Δ values was our segregation index. The Pearson correlation coefficient measures how closely two sets of numbers rise and fall together, on a scale from −1 to 1.

To estimate how similar the expected and test sounds were, we used our experimental data [13] to work out each cell's average change in firing rate over many trials when those sounds were played in the passive condition. We used the same time windows as in the A-M experiment (Fig. 3). For each animal, we made a population firing-rate vector, a list of the firing rates of all its recorded cells. For each pair of sounds (expected and test), we measured how similar the two were as the Pearson correlation between these two vectors (Fig. 4f). In the model, this similarity is calculated from the activity of all the cells that are active for either the expected or the test sound in the passive condition.

### A network with separate excitatory and inhibitory cells

In a network with separate excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) cells, the voltages of the E and I cells change over time according to these equations:

(12) dh_i^E/dt = −h_i^E + ∑_{j=1}^{N_E} J_ij^EE ϕ(h_j^E) + ∑_{j=1}^{N_I} J_ij^EI ϕ_I(h_j^I) + I_i^E
     dh_i^I/dt = −h_i^I + ∑_{j=1}^{N_E} J_ij^IE ϕ(h_j^E) + ∑_{j=1}^{N_I} J_ij^II ϕ_I(h_j^I) + I_i^I

Here N_E and N_I are the numbers of excitatory and inhibitory cells. We assume that the activation function for inhibitory cells is ReLU with a threshold of zero, ϕ_I(x) = max{x, 0}. If we make the E cells' activity at a steady state match the activity of the cells in our original network [Eq. (1)], this puts limits on the connection strengths and the feedforward input (SI §5):

(13) J^EE − J^EI (I + J^II)⁻¹ J^IE = J
     I^E − J^EI (I + J^II)⁻¹ I^I = I^F

Here J and I^F are the connection matrix and feedforward input used in Eq. (1). We also assume that the matrix I + J^II is invertible, which means it has a unique inverse. In general, there are many possible sets of values {J^EE, J^EI, J^IE, J^II, I^E, I^I} that satisfy Eq. (13), so we describe a whole family of solutions. This family runs smoothly between two extremes. At one end is private inhibition, where J^IE is the identity matrix, so each inhibitory cell only holds back other inhibitory cells. At the other end are solutions with an inhibitory internal prediction, where the rows of J^IE are given by the stimulus weight vectors (SI §5). We also show that, apart from a constant factor, the balance level defined earlier [Eq. (7)] is the same as the stimulus-specific, local part of the E/I balance level in the E/I network (SI §5).

We extended the cell types [Eqs. (10) and (11)] to I cells. Here, the average input to inhibitory cells is not 0, so before applying the rules we subtracted the average from the voltage [the h's in Eqs. (10) and (11)].

### Looking at the responses of regular spiking and fast spiking cells

We estimated the connection structure parameter λ^EI from recordings of regular spiking and fast spiking nerve cells [12]. Fast spiking cells are a type of inhibitory cell. Using the same time windows as in Figs. 3b and 4e, f, we worked out each cell's average change in firing rate over many trials in the passive and movement conditions, for the expected sound and for the test sound. For each animal, these firing-rate changes formed eight population vectors: regular or fast spiking, expected or test sound, movement or passive. We calculated the Pearson correlation between the population vectors in the movement and passive conditions, which gave four values for each animal, shown in Fig. 5d. We treated the correlation values for the expected sound as "after learning". We treated the correlation values for the test sound, which was not linked to pressing the lever, as "before learning".

### A layered network model

In the layered network model, each cell belongs to one of three modules, or layers. The small raised numbers in the equations show which module each cell is in:

(14) M1: dh_i^1/dt = −h_i^1(t) + b1 ∑_j J_ij^1 ϕ(h_j^1(t)) + ∑_k W_ik^1 x_k + ∑_{k′} V_ik′^1 ϕ(h_{k′}^2(t))
     M2: dh_i^2/dt = −h_i^2(t) + b2 ∑_j J_ij^2 ϕ(h_j^2(t)) + ∑_k W_ik^2 ϕ(h_k^1(t)) + ∑_{k′} V_ik′^2 ϕ(h_{k′}^3(t))
     M3: dh_i^3/dt = −h_i^3(t) + b3 ∑_j J_ij^3 ϕ(h_j^3(t)) + ∑_k W_ik^3 ϕ(h_k^2(t)) + ∑_{k′} V_ik′^3 y_{k′}

The feedforward and recurrent connections are generalizations of those in the single-module network. In particular, J_ij^l = −b_l/N ∑_k (W_ik^l W_jk^l + V_ik^l V_jk^l). These equations make the prediction errors as small as possible in each module, with predictions running in both directions between modules (Fig. S11a, right; SI §2.3). The model can also be extended to a layered network with any number of layers (SI §2.3).

In Fig. S11, we compare this model with a three-module model in which predictions run in only one direction. In that one-direction model, the activity in each module is governed by:

(15) M1: dh_i^1/dt = −h_i^1(t) + b1 ∑_j J_ij^1u ϕ(h_j^1(t)) + ∑_k W_ik^1 x_k + ∑_{k′} W_ik′^2 ϕ(h_{k′}^2(t))
     M2: dh_i^2/dt = −h_i^2(t) + b2 ∑_j J_ij^2 ϕ(h_j^2(t)) + ∑_k W_ik^2 ϕ(h_k^1(t)) + ∑_{k′} V_ik′^2 ϕ(h_{k′}^3(t))
     M3: dh_i^3/dt = −h_i^3(t) + b3 ∑_j J_ij^3u ϕ(h_j^3(t)) + ∑_k V_ik^2 ϕ(h_k^2(t)) + ∑_{k′} V_ik′^3 y_{k′}

where J_ij^1u = −b_l/N ∑_k W_ik^1 W_jk^1 − δ_ij and J_ij^3u = −b_l/N ∑_k V_ik^3 V_jk^3 − δ_ij. Here δ_ij is 1 when i and j are the same cell and 0 otherwise. These equations make the goal function shown in Fig. S11a, left, as small as possible. In this model, M1 and M3 make predictions of their own stimulus inputs, and M2 makes predictions of the activity in M1 and M3.

### Statistical tests

In Figs. 3c, 4f and 5d, we used two-sided, unpaired t-tests. A t-test checks whether the averages of two groups differ by more than chance alone would usually produce. "Unpaired" means the two groups are made of different cells, and "two-sided" means we looked for a difference in either direction. ⋆ means p < 0.05 and ⋆⋆⋆ means p < 0.0005. A p-value below 0.05 means that if there were really no difference, a gap this large would appear by chance less than 5% of the time.

## Results

### Networks that learn to make predictions about many signals at once

We studied the patterns of activity that build up inside networks of nerve cells connected in loops. These networks make predictions from signals that come from more than one sense and from the animal's own movements. We focused on a typical kind of learning, called associative training. In it, an animal is shown pairs of signals, either at the same time or after a short delay. The two signals in a pair usually come from different senses, such as sound and sight, or one is a sensory signal and the other is a movement, such as sound and running. The animal already knows each part of the pair on its own. So in this kind of learning, we can study the calculations that link the two parts together, and we can watch them being learned over time as the strengths of the connections between cells change.

Our network model has a large number, N, of nerve cells connected in loops. Each cell's firing rate, meaning how fast it fires on average, depends on the electrical current it receives, but not in a simple straight-line way (Fig. 1a). When the network is shown the k-th pair of signals, the values of the two parts of that pair, x_k and y_k, are the values of the two input vectors x and y. We considered situations with P pairs of signals, so x and y each have P values. The strength of the k-th signal reaching each cell is given by the parts of two weight vectors, w_k and v_k. These are lists of N numbers, one for each cell, that describe how strongly each cell responds to that signal. When P is about the same size as N, we say the network makes predictions about many signals at once.

With these definitions, different pairs of signals are orthogonal to each other, which means they do not overlap at all. The number of pairs, P, is the number of signals the network has to handle. We call this "high-dimensional" because the space spanned by all the input vectors has many dimensions. We made this simplifying assumption, that the pairs of signals are not related to each other, so that the mathematics stays manageable.

**Fig. 1. Predictive patterns of activity appear in a network of cells connected in loops as it learns.**

a A network of cells connected in loops, driven by P pairs of signals (x and y). Associative training makes the weights that carry the input signals (w and v) more closely related. The weights of the loops are adjusted together to keep prediction errors small and to encode the signals efficiently overall. With these best loop connections, the network's activity lets us read out which signal was shown, predict a "missing" signal, and measure the prediction error. b Firing rates of single cells in the match and mismatch conditions. At first, the responses in the two conditions are related. After learning, they are less related: match responses are held back and mismatch responses are boosted. c The ratio of average mismatch to match firing rates rises during learning. d A reduced three-dimensional space of network activity. Each arrow shows the firing rates of the cells in one condition and stage of learning, after subtracting the average. e Learning makes the responses to x and to y, when shown separately (blue), point in opposite directions, and makes the responses in the match and mismatch conditions less related (red). Both are measured by the angle between the arrows. f Firing rates of single cells to two pairs of signals in the match and mismatch conditions. In the network we studied (left), the responses to the two signals are not related. In a model where prediction errors and stimulus signals are handled by separate groups of cells (right), they would be strongly related. Circles and error bars in (c, e) show the mean ± 1 standard deviation (a measure of spread) over n = 10 runs of the network in Eq. (1). See Methods for more details.

Before training, the weight vectors for each pair of signals are random and unrelated within the pair (that is, w ⋅ v = 0, where we left out the k for convenience). During training, the two become related (w ⋅ v = μ, with μ > 0). This matches measurements showing that learning reorganizes excitatory connections between cells. The changes in the loop connections are chosen to make the errors between the network's own predictions and the real signals as small as possible, while making the overall encoding as efficient as possible (Methods). Our model extends earlier models of predictive processing, of a type called autoencoders, to handle predictions across several senses. It also fits the idea that predictive processing is a sign of the brain working out hidden variables, such as the state of the world, using Bayesian inference, a way of reasoning that weighs evidence against what is already expected (Methods).

With these assumptions, we worked out exact formulas for the main features of the network's activity for different signals and at different stages of learning. Notably, when the network is very large, these features of the whole network do not depend on the randomness of the starting weights (Methods). The resulting activity lets the network read out which signal was shown, predict the "missing" signal (that is, predict y from x), and measure the prediction error (Fig. 1a). We used these results (SI §2–3) to explore how the network's activity across several senses is organized, and which circuit mechanisms support it.

We first looked at the cells' responses during learning in the match condition (x = y) and the mismatch condition (x ≠ y). We set x and y to be yes-or-no signals: 1 means the signal is present and 0 means it is absent. The signals were sight paired with sound, sight paired with movement (V-M), or sound paired with movement (A-M). Our mathematics also works when more than two signals predict each other, and when the inputs change smoothly, for example the speed of running or of moving scenery (Methods).

Before associative training (μ = 0), most cells in the network respond about equally in the match condition (r_xy) and in the mismatch condition (r_x, r_y) (Fig. 1b). After training (μ = 0.9), match responses are held back while mismatch responses are boosted (Fig. 1b). In the same way, the ratio of average mismatch to match firing rates rises (Fig. 1c), which matches associative learning experiments. So when signal y is present, it holds back the response that signal x alone would cause, and it creates a prediction (or expectation) of x. We interpret the boosted mismatch responses as prediction errors.

During learning, the mismatch responses (r_x, r_y) become anti-correlated (Fig. 1d, e). This means that when y is present, it holds back the response to x alone even more strongly. This anti-correlation does not appear between r_x and r_y of a different pair of signals (Fig. S1a). That suggests the prediction signal set off by y is specific to its partner x, which matches earlier studies. Along with this specific holding back of responses to predictable signals, there is a weaker, general boost that depends on the overall size of the sensory input (SI §3). The match and mismatch responses also become less related during learning (Fig. 1d, e), which matches an earlier study. This suggests that the cells' responses can be used to tell apart the case where x is shown in the match condition and the case where it is shown in the mismatch condition. Notably, because the cells' responses are not a simple straight-line function of their inputs, the match response is not the sum of the two mismatch responses (r_xy ≠ r_x + r_y, Fig. 1d).

Next we looked at the cells' responses when the network is trained on two pairs of signals (P = 2, Fig. 1f). This is a step towards the situation with many signals. Earlier studies proposed that the cells involved in predictive processing are split into separate groups by job. In other words, cells that signal the prediction error for one pair of signals tend to signal the prediction error for other pairs, and the same is true for "representation" cells, which encode the signal itself. If this were true, the responses to two pairs of signals would be strongly related (Fig. 1f, right). However, we found no such relationship in the network of cells connected in loops that we studied (Fig. 1f, left). This means, for example, that a cell that signals the prediction error for pair 1 may respond selectively to signal x "itself" for pair 2. It raises the question of which circuit mechanisms could allow this mixing of response types at the level of single cells.

### Learning and the number of signals decide how well prediction circuits work

We then looked at the circuit mechanisms behind making predictions across several senses, with many signals at once. We split each cell's input into two parts: the feedforward part, which is the real signal, and the recurrent part, which is the network's own prediction (Fig. 2a). Earlier analyses of experiments did the same. To measure how much each part contributes, we followed the research on the balance between excitatory and inhibitory signals. We define the balance level B as the total feedforward input divided by the net input to each cell, in each condition (Fig. 2a). In a later section we show that B is closely linked to the balance between excitatory and inhibitory signals, by extending the model to include separate excitatory and inhibitory groups of cells.

**Fig. 2. The balance between feedforward and loop inputs supports predictive processing.**

a Each cell's input is split into a feedforward part (the real signal) and a recurrent part (the network's own prediction). Each cell's balance level B is the total feedforward input divided by the net input (Methods). b The median of B in the match and mismatch conditions during learning (left; the shaded area shows the interquartile range, the spread of the middle half of the values). "Snapshots" of the spread of B early and late in learning show that the match and mismatch conditions become separate (right). The arrows on the x-axis mark the most common value of B early in learning. c A sketch of the curved (nonlinear) change from the space of signals (left) to the space of network activity (center), which makes it possible to read out the relevant features of the signals with a straight-line (linear) calculation. Here, this means telling whether x is shown in the match or mismatch condition. d Error of a support vector machine (SVM), a computer method that learns to sort cases into groups, trained to tell the match and mismatch conditions apart using the input (black) and the cells' responses (green). After learning, a straight-line calculation based on the average firing rate (blue) works almost as well as the best possible method. Data are shown as mean ± 1 standard deviation over n = 10 repeats. e How we find the best balance level, b*. Raising b widens the gap between match and mismatch responses (making them easier to tell apart) but raises the firing rates (bottom). The best balance level B* is found by setting a lower limit on the average firing rate in the mismatch condition and making it as small as possible in the match condition. f As the number of signals grows, B* falls, meaning the balance becomes looser (line: median; shaded area: interquartile range). At α = 0, we fit B* to experimental data (Methods, ref. 20).

During associative learning, the network's own predictions become more accurate. This lets the loop feedback, which carries the prediction signals, cancel out the feedforward signal more reliably. So the overall balance level rises in the match condition but falls in the mismatch condition (Fig. 2b, left). Such changes in the overall balance level have been suggested as the reason why the whole network responds to "rare" signals. Notice that at first, the spread of balance levels (across cells and signals) is similar in the match and mismatch conditions, but becomes significantly different late in learning (Fig. 2b, right). Indeed, after learning, the most common value of B is about 0 in the mismatch condition, which explains the strong prediction-error responses.

To understand what balance does when predictions span several senses, we looked at how it affects the curved (nonlinear) change the network makes from the input signals to its activity (Fig. 2c). The network's connections are tuned to make predictions across several senses, rather than prediction errors (Methods). Even so, the shape of the cells' responses after training makes it easy to read out the prediction errors. In particular, a straight-line calculation cannot read out the prediction error from the input signal, but it can once the input has been changed by the network's curved response (Fig. 2d; Methods). Moreover, although the prediction error itself depends on the signal, the calculation that reads it out can be the same for every signal after learning. A calculation that uses only the average firing rate works about as well as the best possible method, a support vector machine tuned to each signal (Fig. 2d). This suggests that the shape the network learns lets it use the same calculation for all pairs of signals, without "re-learning".

Because this curved change is so important for predictive processing, we next focused on the overall nonlinear gain, b (Methods, ref. 43). We found that raising b raises the average firing rates in both the match and mismatch conditions, while also widening the gap between them (Fig. 2e, top). So a large b makes prediction errors easier to read out, at the cost of more activity overall. Since b is a property of the network itself and could in principle be adjusted as things change, we set out to find the best value, which we call b*. Specifically, we required the average network response in the mismatch condition to be above a certain threshold, while requiring a small but nonzero average response in the match condition (Fig. 2e). This fits reports of weak responses to predictable signals. The resulting b* gives the best balance level B*, which supports efficient encoding and reliable reading out (Fig. 2e, bottom).

We carried out this search for the best value for networks trained to predict signals from sets with more and more signals. We measured this with α = P/N, the number of pairs divided by the number of cells. We used the same firing-rate limits, chosen so that B* at α = 0 matches experimental data. We also assumed that an "over-trained" animal learns a single pair of signals (that is, α = 1/N ≈ 0). Surprisingly, we found that the best balance level falls as α rises (Fig. 2f). This effect holds up against noise and against changes in the statistics of the signals (Fig. S1b, c). This drop in balance limits the interference between the network's own predictions for the larger number of pairs of signals (Methods). We therefore expect networks making predictions in natural conditions (large α) to have a "loose" balance, which keeps the overall interference from learning many internal predictions as small as possible.

We used recordings of brain activity from animals trained on sight paired with movement (V-M) and on sound paired with movement (A-M) to pin down our network model. Specifically, we assume that the circuit in the matching sensory area works at the best balance level. Using the link between the network's activity and its balance levels after training, we estimated the balance levels in the mouse sensory cortex (Methods). In the V-M experiment, mice were trained to link their running speed with the speed of moving scenery in virtual reality (Fig. 3a). The voltage of cells in the primary visual cortex was recorded from inside the cells, in the match and mismatch conditions. Fitting the average voltage change in the two conditions to the model gives an estimated balance level of B*_V-M = 162 ± 61. We got a consistent result in the A-M experiment, where mice were trained to press a lever and heard sound feedback that followed their presses (Fig. 3b, c). Here the recording was made from outside the cells, so fitting B* needed a slightly changed procedure (Methods).

**Fig. 3. Estimating the balance level from experiments on predictive processing.**

a A sketch of a learned link between running and moving scenery in virtual reality. Voltages of different cells (n = 32 cells) in the primary visual cortex show that they respond to the mismatch between running speed and moving scenery (prediction errors). b A sketch of a learned link between pressing a lever and hearing a sound. Cells' firing rates show that they respond to sounds played without a lever press (passive, prediction errors) and with a lever press (movement). Data from n = 8 animals. c The median best balance level for the V-M (blue) and A-M (red) experiments is similar. We assume α = 0 because, in both experiments, the animals were trained extensively on a single pair of signals. Error bars come from taking subsamples (n = 100 repeats, Methods). We used two-sided, unpaired t-tests (p = 0.12). Circles and error bars: mean ± 1 standard deviation.

Notably, the balance level estimates were consistent across animals (Fig. S2) and across laboratories (Fig. 3), even though the experiments studied different brain areas and senses and used different methods. These factors may affect the balance level to some degree. However, our analysis predicts that the balance level can fall by up to tenfold when the number of signals grows (Fig. 2e and Fig. S1b, c). This prediction could be confirmed if future experiments find a looser balance in animals used to rich sensory surroundings.

### In the model, signals and prediction errors are not kept apart

We next looked at how the different kinds of responses are organized inside the network. Earlier work proposed that predictive processing circuits contain two separate groups of cells: (i) "representation" (R) cells, which "faithfully" represent outside sensory signals and encode the network's own predictions, and (ii) "prediction-error" (PE) cells, which signal the difference between the real input and the network's own predictions. Our network model also has cells that respond selectively to these signals, so we wondered whether they form separate groups. We used the same rules for sorting cells that experimental studies use (Methods, refs. 2, 60). R cells are those that respond strongly and similarly in the match and mismatch conditions, while PE cells are those that respond strongly in the mismatch condition but weakly in the match condition (Fig. 4a). These rules for R and PE responses depend on the signal: the same cell may respond differently to different pairs of signals. We also note that the rule for PE cells used in the experimental studies differs from the one used in classic predictive processing studies. In those studies, a "prediction error cell" is a specific computing unit dedicated to comparing top-down predictions with bottom-up sensory inputs. We use the experimental rule to connect our model results to experimental data, and to show how the way prediction errors are calculated differs between our network and models with dedicated groups of error cells. Still, the two rules are related. A dedicated group of "error" cells, as proposed in classic studies, would always count as PE cells under the experimental rule and would never count as R cells for any pair of signals.

**Fig. 4. Signals and errors are mixed, not kept apart, in networks that make predictions about many signals at once.**

a A sketch of the typical response patterns of different cell types to the signals x and y. b The share of representation (R) and prediction-error (PE) cells in the model at different stages of learning. Error bars: 1 standard deviation over n = 10 runs of the network. c The spread of each cell's Δ value, the difference between its mismatch and match responses to two particular pairs of signals. Only cells that respond to both pairs are included (Methods). Mixed cells have significantly different Δ values for the two pairs, that is, they fall in the blue rectangles. d How the number of signals affects mixed cells. The share of mixed cells rises as the number of signals grows (left). The share of dedicated PE cells falls as the number of signals grows. See SI §6 for the definition of dedicated PE cells. Circles: mean; error bars: 1 standard deviation over n = 200 runs of the network. e Testing whether signals and prediction errors are kept apart, using recordings from a learned link between sound and movement. Shown are the Δ values of signal-responsive cells for the expected sound and each probe sound (colors). The length and direction of the long and short axes of the red ellipses show the size and direction of the two main patterns in the data (n = 5 animals). f The segregation index plotted against how similar the expected and probe sounds are, for different pairs of expected and probe sounds. Colored points are subsamples of the data, and crosses are the average for each probe type (Methods). We compare the experimental data with the matching quantities from the model, by changing how sparse the model's responses are (f, see SI §4).

Using these rules, we first worked out the shares of R and PE cells when the network learns a single pair of signals (P = 1, Fig. 4b). As training goes on, the share of PE cells rises significantly, which matches experiments and the idea that the network learns to "recognize" the pair of signals. This result does not depend on the sorting rule (Fig. S3). The share of R cells stays the same (Fig. 4b), although we note that the trend does depend on the rule (Fig. S3).

We next asked how cells respond to more complex sets of signals, namely two learned pairs. The idea that predictive processing is split into separate groups says that if a cell is a PE cell for pair 1, and it is active when signals from pair 2 are shown, it will probably count as a PE cell for those signals too. To test this idea, we worked out the spread of cells' responses in the four relevant conditions (mismatch/match × pair 1/pair 2), and sorted each cell as R or PE separately for each pair (Methods). We started with the situation with few signals, where the two pairs are the only ones the network has learned (P = 2, α = P/N ≈ 0). Surprisingly, with the settings pinned down by the data, although many cells belong to the same type for both pairs, about 25% of cells are actually mixed: they count as different types for the two pairs (Fig. 4c, left).

On top of that, as the network learns more signals, the share of mixed cells doubles (Fig. 4c, d). The idea is that a loose balance between the many feedforward and loop inputs leads to a wide spread of balance levels across the network (Fig. S4a). That wide spread, in turn, gives each cell the freedom to encode different features for different pairs of signals. The share of mixed cells in Fig. 4d is for two particular pairs of signals. When we looked at the whole set of learned signals instead, most cells were mixed for at least two pairs (Fig. S4b). Moreover, the share of cells that encode only prediction errors falls as the number of signals grows (Fig. 4d, right). So cells that mix signals and prediction errors are common in the network, while dedicated prediction-error cells become more and more rare, especially when there are many signals.

### Experimental evidence that predictions and signals are mixed

We then turned to testing this key prediction of our network model, by looking for signs of mixed signals and predictions in experimental data. In our recent work, we recorded responses in the primary auditory cortex of mice trained to link a simple action, pressing a lever, with a simple outcome, a predictable tone. After extensive training, we recorded from outside the cells in the auditory cortex while the animals heard probe sounds. These sounds differed from the expected sound in various ways, and the animals either pressed the lever or heard the tone passively (Fig. 4e).

We analyzed this data as follows. For each cell, we worked out the difference (Δ) between its mismatch response (passive: sound only) and its match response (active: lever press + sound) (Fig. 4e, bottom), much as we did for the model (Fig. 4c). For each of the four probe sounds, "match" means a lever press paired with that probe sound, and "mismatch" means the response after the probe sound without a lever press. We expected the Δ values of mixed cells to sit in the upper left or lower right corners of the plot (as in the blue rectangles in Fig. 4c). That would mean cells whose match and mismatch responses are similar for the expected sound but different for the probe sound, or the other way round.

We measured how mixed, or how far from being kept apart, the predictive representation is, by working out the Pearson correlation coefficient of the Δ values for the expected sound and for each probe sound separately (Fig. 4e). A correlation coefficient measures how closely two sets of numbers rise and fall together. We call this coefficient the segregation index. It is close to 1 if the Δ values are strongly related across the two pairs of signals (expected and probe). A segregation index close to 0 means that the signals and predictions are "maximally mixed". We also worked out how similar the expected and probe sounds are, as the correlation between the cells' responses to them. Crucially, this similarity was based on responses recorded in a separate part of the experiment, when sounds were played passively, not after a lever press. If cells fall into two separate groups, the segregation index should be close to 1, whatever the similarity between the sounds. Instead, we found that the segregation index depends strongly on how similar the sounds are (Fig. 4f).

When the expected and probe sounds are similar (Fig. 4e, f, green shades), the segregation index is close to 1, although a random subsampling analysis shows a statistically significant effect of sound similarity on the segregation index. When the probe differs more from the expected sound (Fig. 4e, f, orange), the segregation index drops sharply to about 0.5 (P < 0.0005, two-sided unpaired t-test; Methods). A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no effect, a difference this large would rarely appear by chance alone. The link we found between sound similarity and how mixed the responses are fits the prediction of our network model with mixed responses, at a suitable level of sparsity (Fig. 4f). The segregation index depends significantly on sound similarity, and it is well below 1. Together, these suggest that predictive processing is mixed in the mouse auditory cortex. We found a similar relationship when we calculated the Δ values from the "complementary" mismatch response, based on the response to a lever press with no sound, rather than to a sound with no lever press (Fig. S5).

We note that this analysis is an indirect test of the model's prediction that signals and predictions are mixed. Indeed, the mixing in the model involves two learned pairs of signals (Fig. 4c), while in the experiment the animal was trained on only the expected sound. Even so, the lower segregation index we found for probe sounds very different from the expected sound gives strong evidence against the idea that the predictive processing circuit is split into separate groups of cells. The modeling approach we used here gives a way to produce ideas that can be tested more directly in future experiments.

### Predictions about short-lived signals from several senses

Until now, we assumed that the input signals change slowly compared with the network's activity, and we used this to work out the features of steady-state predictive representations, meaning the patterns of activity once things have settled. Here, we look at how the predictive representations change over time when the network is shown signals that change quickly. We studied the network's responses to short pulses of pairs of signals under three conditions: x only, y only, and match (Fig. 5a). Crucially, in the match condition the x and y pulses are separated by a gap, Δt. So the network does not get the two signals at the same time, and it must make and hold on to the prediction of y after signal x has gone. This is similar to our experiments, where the predictable sound comes a certain time after the lever press.

We found that after learning, a slower timescale appears in the network's responses (Fig. 5a). This timescale is not there before learning, and it could support predictions that last longer but are still short-lived. Indeed, on this slow timescale, the average firing rate is held back in the match condition compared with the mismatch conditions (x only, y only), especially for small Δt (Fig. 5a). This holding back depends on the signal: it is missing when x and y from different pairs are shown (compare the solid and dashed purple curves in Fig. 5a). We also found that the holding back of responses in the match condition grows during learning, and depends strongly on the timing between the paired signals (Fig. 5b). These features of the model match our measurements of links between movement and sound, especially our experiments in which we shifted the timing of these links.

**Fig. 5. Short-lived changes in activity in networks that make predictions.**

a Average firing rates in response to mismatched pulses fall quickly before learning and slowly after learning (μ = 0 and 0.9, respectively). The response in the match condition is held back when the gap between signals is short (Δt = 0.01). The response to matched x and y signals from different pairs (dashed) overlaps with the mismatch responses. b The ratio of average mismatch to match responses, plotted against the stage of learning and the gap between signals, measured after the signals are removed (blue circles in (a)). Inset: the timescale over which responses fade grows during learning. Line: mean; error bars: 1 standard deviation over n = 10 runs of the network. c Sketch of the short-lived paths of network activity caused by signals in the mismatch and match conditions. After learning, the paths stay far apart even after the signals are removed, suggesting that learning makes the two conditions easier to tell apart. d The spread of each cell's Δ values over time, the difference between its mismatch and match responses to two particular pairs of signals. Shown are the spreads at two time points, matching the gray, blue and green symbols in (c). Thick and thin lines enclose 50% and 80% of the spread. Only cells that respond to both pairs are included (Methods). e The numbers of mixed cells and of x-response cells over time, for different numbers of signals α. As the number of signals grows, the total number of mixed cells rises and stays high for longer.

To understand these short-lived predictions better than the average firing rate alone, we calculated a readout direction, Δr(t), that depends on time and on the signal. It is the difference between the firing rate vectors in the two signal conditions (Fig. 5c). As with the average firing rates, after learning the size of Δr(t) fades slowly, which means the network keeps its predictions for each signal. To see how the number of signals affects the cell types in the network, we worked out the spread of Δ values over time, the difference between mismatch and match responses, for two pairs of signals (Fig. 5d). When we sorted cells into types using the same rules, we found that the number of mixed cells in the network changes over time. Just as in our analysis of the steady-state responses, the number of mixed cells rises as the number of signals grows (Fig. 5e).

We also tested our network model with step inputs of limited width (Fig. S6). Remarkably, the readout directions we used to tell the signal conditions apart, and the sorting of cells into types, which we had worked out from steady-state responses, still work here. Cells that are R or PE for a particular pair of signals at steady state usually belong to the same type during the short-lived responses. An important advantage of this kind of changing input is that it let us study how the balance level changes over time in different signal conditions. This cannot be done with pulses, because there is no feedforward input during them. After learning, the network shows a short-lived tight balance after the second (predicted) signal starts (Fig. S6c). The peak of the balance level during this period falls as the number of signals grows (Fig. S6d), just as for the steady-state predictive representation (Fig. 2f). Taken together, our results show that the mechanisms behind predictive calculations, and the features of predictions about many signals that we identified from steady-state responses, also hold when signals are shown for only a short time.

We tested how robust the calculations in our network model are when connections are randomly cut, which makes the connections lopsided (Fig. S7). In this sparse network, activity keeps fluctuating even when the input signals stay the same, which matches an earlier study. Despite these strong fluctuations in single cells' activity, the network's own prediction for each signal stays stable (Fig. S7). In the sparse network, adding more signals leads to a looser balance and a larger share of mixed cells (Fig. S7).

### Predictive processing in networks with excitatory and inhibitory cells

So far, we have focused on linking the model's responses to measurements of excitatory cells' activity. In our network, each cell's connections could be both excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I), so it does not follow Dale's law, the rule that a cell sends only one kind of signal. Because more and more studies look at the role of inhibitory cells in making predictions, we wanted to link our model results more closely to experiments by extending the model to a network with separate E and I cells. We did this by requiring that the E cells in the E/I network had exactly the same activity as the cells in the original model. This guarantees that the E cells have the predictive processing properties we have studied so far, and it lets us study what the I cells do.

The connections in the E/I network have four parts, for connections to and from E and I cells (Fig. 6). We used a method called non-negative matrix factorization to "solve" for these parts (Methods, refs. 64, 65). The balance level B, defined earlier from feedforward and loop inputs (Fig. 2), equals the signal-specific part of the E/I balance in the E/I networks (SI §5).

**Fig. 6. An E/I model pinned down by data suggests that the network's own predictions are spread across the network.**

a A sketch of the E/I network. Excitatory cells receive outside inputs, and their activity is required to equal that of the cells in our original model. b A family of E/I network solutions, set by the value λEI. c The cosine similarity (cosψI) between the match and mismatch inhibitory responses to signal x (r_xy, r_x), for different values of μ and λEI (left). Error bars: 1 standard deviation over n = 200 runs. d The matching correlation between the responses of two groups of cells, regular-spiking (RS) and fast-spiking (FS) cells, from n = 8 animals in ref. 12. Each point is data from one animal. The mean ± 1 standard deviation across animals is also shown. RS cells become significantly less related during learning (p = 0.025), while the correlation of FS cells does not change (p = 0.31, two-sided unpaired t-test). e The angle θI (left) between the inhibitory responses to the paired signals in the mismatch conditions (r_x, −r_y), the angle ψI′ (center) between the match and mismatch inhibitory responses to signal y (r_xy, r_y), and the share of inhibitory R cells (right). Error bars: 1 standard deviation over n = 20 runs. f The spread of connection strengths of all I-to-E connections before and after learning, when λEI = 0 (left), and for pairs of E and I cells of particular types (R to R, middle; PE to R or PE, right). g The same as (f), when the inhibitory structure is matched to data (λEI = 0.6). Here, learning makes inhibitory connections sparser and weaker. Connections between R cells stay very small throughout learning.

This mathematical method did not give a single connection pattern. Instead, we found a family of connection patterns, all meeting the requirements, that depends on one setting, λEI. This setting moves between two extremes of structured E/I connections (Fig. 6b). At one extreme (λEI = 0), inhibition is "private": each "parent" E cell connects to a single "daughter" I cell, with equal activity. Earlier predictive processing models with lateral inhibition assumed this without saying so. At the other extreme (λEI = 1), each I cell receives many excitatory inputs and signals an "internal prediction" of one signal the network has learned, much like earlier models with separate groups of cells. We explored the whole range of inhibitory representations between these extremes using the same approach as for E cells (Figs. 1b–e and 4b).

We started by comparing the inhibitory responses to signal x in the match (r_xy) and mismatch (r_x) conditions, at different stages of learning (Fig. 6c). Before learning (μ = 0), raising λEI makes the inhibitory responses clearly less aligned. After learning (μ ≈ 1), raising λEI has an effect on alignment that does not keep going in one direction. Intriguingly, at λEI = 1, after learning, the I responses in the two conditions are more aligned than the E responses (Fig. 6c, compare green and black for μ = 1).

These features let us estimate λEI from measurements of regular-spiking (RS, probably excitatory) and fast-spiking (FS, probably inhibitory) cells. To do this, we worked out the correlation between the match and mismatch responses in the auditory cortex, separately for RS and FS cells recorded in ref. 12, and compared these correlations with the model before and after learning (Fig. 6d). Specifically, we treated the pairing of movement with a probe sound (not played during training) as "before learning", and the pairing of movement with the expected sound as "after learning" (Methods). For RS cells, the correlation fell significantly during learning, which matches the change in the model's E cells' responses (Fig. 6c, blue circles). For FS cells, by contrast, the correlation did not change significantly during learning, which rules out small values of λEI. Moreover, the correlation after learning was similar for RS and FS cells, which rules out large values of λEI. Taken together, our analysis suggests that an in-between value of λEI ≈ 0.6 best captures the experimental observations. This fits the idea of "promiscuous" inhibitory connections, which link many cells and help hold back responses to expected signals.

With this value pinned down by experiments (λEI = 0.6), our theory makes testable predictions about inhibitory prediction representations. First, we expect the mismatch I responses (x only, y only) to be significantly less anti-aligned than the E responses in the same conditions (Fig. 6e, left; Fig. 1d, e). Second, we predict that inhibitory responses in the match condition and in the y-only mismatch condition are strongly related (Fig. 6e, middle), more so than for E responses. In the model, the lopsidedness of r_x ⋅ r_xy and r_y ⋅ r_xy may in the future be linked to the different jobs of different types of inhibitory cells. Third, the share of I cells with R responses falls moderately during learning, compared with E cells. We note, however, that the share of E cells with R responses depends moderately on the threshold, especially before learning (Fig. S8). This may make it hard to detect differences between E and I cells in the share of cells with R responses.

Earlier work on predictive processing suggested that associative learning strengthens top-down inhibitory connections from outside the local circuit. These would cancel the bottom-up excitation and hold back responses in the match condition. So we wondered which changes in inhibitory connections during learning lead to the signal-specific holding back of activity in our E/I network model. One possibility is that the inhibitory connections that predict the signal are strengthened. Another is that inhibition is reorganized more subtly, so that inhibitory signals are spread out differently before and after learning.

We calculated the spread of I-to-E connection strengths before and after learning in the family of E/I network models. When inhibition is private (λEI = 0), this spread widens during learning (Fig. 6f). Looking at how the connection strengths change depending on the type of the sending and receiving cells (R or PE) suggests that the signal-specific holding back of E responses comes from strengthened I connections from cells that "faithfully" represent the signal. In other words, when inhibition is private, the prediction signal comes partly from stronger connections from inhibitory R cells to excitatory cells (Fig. S9). By contrast, when the inhibitory structure was matched to experimental data (λEI = 0.6), learning makes I connections sparser overall (Fig. 6g). Interestingly, here R-to-R connections can either grow or shrink, unlike when λEI = 0 (compare the middle panels of Fig. 6f, g). Moreover, when λEI = 0.6, inhibitory connections from PE cells, which are very weak at first, become strongly strengthened.

Together, our results suggest that (i) predictive processing is learned without large increases in the average strength of inhibitory connections. We also saw this for other values of λEI (Fig. S10). (ii) The "strategy" for learning predictive processing can differ a lot, and depends on the underlying circuit structure (different values of λEI in the model). (iii) When the inhibitory structure is matched to data, the "internal model" is spread widely across the network, and, surprisingly, it comes partly from strengthened connections from inhibitory cells that signal prediction errors. Another sign of this spread-out strategy is that the total inhibitory input to each excitatory cell falls during learning (Fig. S10). This suggests that predictions are mainly calculated by the loop circuitry rather than directly from top-down inputs.

### Predictive representations in layered brain networks

Sensory areas of the brain are built in layers, and different layers respond differently in associative learning tasks. In tasks that involve predicting what the senses and our own movements will tell us, it has been suggested that movement-related input comes from movement areas and first enters the primary sensory area through the deep layers (L5/6). On the other hand, sensory input from the outside world first enters the primary sensory area through L4, which then projects to L2/3, where the bottom-up and top-down inputs are combined and processed. To study how this layer structure affects predictive processing, we extended our network model, which has a single block and no layers, to a network with three blocks connected in loops (Fig. 7). During associative learning, the network receives paired inputs from different senses. Crucially, the first block (M1) receives input from one sense, and the last block (M3) receives input from the other sense (Fig. 7a). Unlike earlier studies, each block in this network makes predictions in both directions, for inputs from the level above and below it in the hierarchy. For example, M2 predicts the activity in M1, at the same time as M1 predicts the activity in M2. So this layered model can also be used for processing across different brain areas that swap prediction signals in both directions (for example, the auditory and visual cortices, ref. 16), not just for the layer structure within one brain area.
