We first studied the effects of the gain settings for each block. After learning, the average mismatch responses rise steadily with b1 and b2 (Fig. 7b). We required the average mismatch response to be above a certain threshold and made the match responses as small as possible for each block. This gave a continuous set of combinations of settings that meet these requirements (Fig. 7b, magenta line). We fixed b2 so that the share of prediction error cells in M2 after learning is similar to the share in the single-block model (Fig. 3b), which also fixes b1 and b3 (Fig. 7b, star). With these settings, we looked at how associative learning shapes the network's representations in the different blocks.

In the x-only mismatch condition (x = 1, y = 0), the overall mismatch responses rise during learning, with clear differences between blocks (Fig. 7c). Cells in M1, which receive the x signal directly, respond remarkably similarly in the match and mismatch conditions throughout learning. In contrast, cells in M3 respond mainly to signal y but gradually become tuned to signal x as learning goes on. Cells in M2 have the largest mismatch-to-match response ratio and develop the strongest prediction error responses after learning.

To show the role of predictions in both directions, we compared the responses across the two senses in our layered model with a model that makes predictions in only one direction (Fig. S11). In the one-direction model, M2 predicts the activity in M1 and M3, but M1 or M3 makes no "backward" predictions to M2. Making these one-way prediction errors as small as possible means the network is optimizing a different goal, and this gives a different structure and activity from a model with predictions in both directions (Fig. S11a). We set the settings of the two models to be the same to make the comparison easy. We found that cells in M1 and M2 of both models respond in similar ways in the match and x-only mismatch conditions. However, in the one-direction model, the responses of cells in M3 are only weakly affected by signal x, which comes from the other sense (Fig. S11b). In the two-direction model, by contrast, M3 develops strong responses to the signal from the other sense (Fig. 7c). As a result, our analyses of reading out the information confirm that, across various signal conditions, M3's activity carries much less information about the signal sent to M1 in the one-direction model than in the two-direction model we propose (Fig. S11c). So making predictions in both directions strengthens the exchange of information across brain areas. This fits recent experimental findings that movement areas encode sound information, and that prediction signals are swapped back and forth between visual and auditory areas.

Next, we sorted the cells in each block into types. Before learning, cells that respond to signal x regardless of y (x-response cells) are concentrated in M1, the block that receives the x signal directly. During learning, x-response cells also appear in M2 and M3, although their overall share falls from M1 to M3 (Fig. 7d). PE cells are very rare at first and appear in all blocks during learning, with the largest share in M2 (Fig. 7e). These results match the activity of cells in different layers of the primary sensory cortex.

Finally, we looked at the network's responses to two pairs of signals. As in the single-block model, mixed cells appear in all blocks after learning (Fig. 7f, g). The share of mixed cells is highest in M2, and it rises with the number of learned pairs of signals (Fig. 7f, g). As in the single-block network (Fig. 4d, right), the share of dedicated error cells in M2 falls quickly as the number of signals grows (Fig. 7g, right). We also found that this stronger mixing of signals and prediction errors comes with a significant fall in the median balance level in that block (Fig. 7h). This suggests that a loose balance is the circuit mechanism behind the mixed predictive responses of single cells. Unlike in M2, the share of mixed cells and the median balance level in M1 and M3 do not depend strongly on the number of signals. These results show how the brain's structure shapes what the network does. In particular, we found that different blocks have different shares of representation and prediction error cells, which reminds us of recent experimental findings. Even so, despite these differences, signals and prediction errors are not kept apart in any block after learning.

## Discussion

We wanted to understand how the brain builds an inner 'world model' that guides behavior in everyday, natural conditions. To do this, we studied a family of computer models of brain networks in which nerve cells are connected in loops. These networks learn to make predictions that involve many signals at once, from more than one sense. Our mathematical analysis shows the key ways these networks manage to make such predictions. It also produces new ideas that experiments can test about how the matching brain circuits work. And it gives a way to measure and analyze recordings from large numbers of nerve cells.

Our results build on earlier studies of how the brain represents signals from a single sense. They also offer clues about how responses to several senses are organized inside the first brain areas that handle each sense, as recent experiments have observed. Our approach also lets us add information about the different types of nerve cells and about how the brain is wired. This can help reveal what each type of cell does in making predictions.

We chose a network with loops for two reasons. First, the brain circuits that do predictive processing are known to be full of loops. When the connections in these loops change over time, they form working groups of nerve cells. Earlier work suggested that such groups are what let animals tell apart signals that matter for behavior. Second, predictions about what the senses will tell us usually unfold over time. The natural rhythm of a network with loops can handle this easily.

To keep the mathematics manageable, we designed our network to make predictions once it has settled into a steady state, meaning its activity has stopped changing. We showed that our network also makes predictions when the signals change over time. Importantly, the same mechanisms that support these predictions in the steady state also work when the signals change (Fig. 5). An interesting next step for future research would be to take our results, which assume the network's wiring is fixed in advance, and extend them to networks that learn predictions continuously as they go.

Our results suggest that a balance between two kinds of input can lead to reliable inner predictions within small local circuits. One kind of input is feedforward input, which flows in one direction from one area to another. The other is recurrent input, which loops back within the same area. The same idea also applies to the balance between excitatory and inhibitory signals. Earlier studies of predictive processing models have suggested this too.

An important new prediction from our analysis is this. When these models are extended to realistic conditions, with many signals from several senses, there is a best balance, and it is not infinite. The more signals a prediction involves, the lower this best balance becomes (Fig. 2). Our theory also suggests that a network with an infinitely high balance could be especially easily thrown off by noise when it handles many signals at once.

In real experiments, the balance between excitatory and inhibitory signals varies a great deal from one experiment to another. Based on our results, we propose that this may be a sign of differences in the sets of signals the animals were exposed to. Our results in Figs. 2 and 3 suggest that this idea could be tested step by step, by exposing animals to richer and richer sensory surroundings. Here too, the way the network changes over time may matter. Delays in the connections between cells may affect the best balance in circuits that make predictions involving only a few signals.

The role of this balance in making predictions matters for two things: where the prediction signals come from, and how long it takes to learn them.

(i) Earlier work has shown that predictions linking different senses often depend on the particular signals involved. For example, signals from one brain area can dampen the response to one particular predictable signal in another area. One case is activity in the motor cortex, which controls movement, dampening responses in the visual cortex. It is worth noting that in our model, these calculations happen without fine-tuning the long-distance connections between brain areas. Instead, the loops within the 'receiving' area can pick out the predictions from the long-distance inputs. These inputs are 'promiscuous', meaning they are spread widely across the receiving area. The loops rely on the balance between excitatory and inhibitory signals, and on the way connections change in response to activity.

(ii) In the same brain area, prediction errors can appear after very different lengths of training, from as little as minutes to days. We believe that the many different ways the balance can be set up may explain this wide range of learning times. These include firing-rate adaptation, where cells get used to a steady level of activity; synaptic scaling, where the strength of all a cell's connections is adjusted together; and Hebbian plasticity, where connections grow stronger when the cells on both sides fire together (see the review in ref. 53). Future work may show that our model can also explain how predictions appear over shorter times than those in the experiments we considered here. If so, it could be applied to predictive processing circuits in brain areas below the cortex, and in animals without a backbone.

An important finding of our work is that prediction signals and signals about the outside world are mixed together. Nerve cells that report prediction errors for one pair of signals may also faithfully report whether a second pair of signals is present. In experiments where animals were given several kinds of unexpected sounds, we found signs of this mixing at the level of single cells in the mouse auditory cortex, the brain area that handles hearing (Fig. 4).

To measure this, we used a segregation index, a number that shows how cleanly two kinds of signals are kept apart. In the data, this index differed from what we would expect if the cells were split into separate groups, each doing one job. This difference was statistically significant. That means that if the cells really were split into separate groups, a difference this large would rarely appear by chance alone. Instead, the data support a mixed picture, with signals about the sounds and signals about errors mixed together in layer 2/3 of the primary auditory cortex. This is one of the inner layers of the cortex, where many of the cortex's loops are found.

Our current work explains this mixing in the data in a general way, using a model of how the circuit works (Fig. 4f). However, our analysis of the data does not rule out the possibility that dedicated prediction-error cells exist in other types of cells that were not recorded in our dataset. Future experiments that record a wider variety of cell types will be needed to test this. Another recent study in mice that performed several standard movement actions found mixed signals across the neocortex, the main part of the cortex. These signals combined information about the movements with prediction errors about rewards, as our network model suggests for situations with many signals. An interesting next step would be to use a 'normative' approach, which asks what the best possible design for a task would be. This could explore whether mixing movement signals, sensory predictions and reward predictions brings any advantages, and how much this mixing depends on the details of the task.

Earlier work often assumed, directly, that separate groups of nerve cells carry predictions and prediction errors. We took a different approach, similar to classic 'sparse coding' models, which do not make this assumption. We found that the resulting network with loops ends up with mixed signals as a direct result of how it learns. It learns by making the prediction errors as small as possible, while keeping its total activity within a limit. In this model, prediction errors are worked out across many cells through the loops, using a circuit mechanism that is different from models with separate groups of cells.

Our findings are related to a growing body of research on 'mixed selectivity'. In mixed selectivity, a single nerve cell responds to several features of a signal in complex ways. Even a random network can show mixed selectivity. But in such a network, the pattern of each cell's responses has no structure, so reading out the information that matters for a task requires a decoder that is finely tuned. A decoder is a way of turning the activity of many cells into a single piece of information. Here, we report nerve cells that are mixed in their responses to inner predictions about sensory signals and movement signals (Figs. 4–6). Crucially, the signals the model learns are highly structured. This lets different features of a signal be read out without having to 're-learn' the decoder (Fig. 2).

In our network model, and in recordings from the auditory cortex, nerve cells are mixed in their responses to sounds and to prediction errors. But the auditory cortex also contains nerve cells that carry prediction errors more specifically. Notably, how mixed a cell's responses to sounds and errors are could also differ from one layer of the cortex to another. Our network model, which has layers stacked on top of each other, reproduces this (Fig. 7). The layered model also suggests that this layer-by-layer difference comes from the way the balance changes from layer to layer. This would be an interesting prediction to test in future experiments.

Recent work in the mouse visual cortex found specific genetic markers that are more common in nerve cells that carry positive prediction errors than in those that carry negative ones. However, the studies used different methods and analyzed their data over different time spans, which makes direct comparisons hard. Also, these experiments involved learning a single link between signals, so it is hard to tell apart cells that mix signals and errors with cells that carry only errors. It remains possible that the sensory cortex holds a varied mix of nerve cells: some that share the job of carrying both signals and errors, and others that carry only one or the other. Future experiments in which animals learn several links will be needed to answer this question more directly.

We focused on a network that responds to 'one-hot' or 'tabular' signals. In these signals, each signal is a separate, independent option, like a row in a table, so that no two signals are linked. We chose this kind of signal because of the signals used in recent experiments. It let us learn about the role of the circuit's structure in predictive processing, without the effects of changing how the signals are related. We showed that our results also hold when the signals are mixed with noise that is not linked to the signals (Fig. S1). However, the simple signals we used do not capture the complex ways that many signals in natural scenes are linked to each other. A full theoretical account of more general kinds of signals, building on our analysis, is an important direction for future research. It would also need more experiments, in which animals are trained to do more complex tasks.

In summary, predictive processing is a widespread and basic calculation that supports many kinds of behavior in many animal species. Here, we take a first step towards closing the gap between the theory of predictive processing with many signals from several senses, and recordings from brain circuits in experiments on predictive processing. Our results show what particular circuit patterns and mechanisms do in making such predictions. More broadly, our work will help explain how the brain builds complex inner models. It does this by shedding light on what biological predictive processing circuits have in common with artificial systems, and how they differ, especially with artificial systems trained using self-supervised methods, which learn from data without being given the right answers.
